paragraphs: In the forenoon the fight is even, but Agamemnon swings the day toward the Achaeans until he is wounded and leaves the field—Hector then drives all before him until Diomedes wounds him—Paris wounds Diomedes—Odysseus, Nestor, and Idomeneus do astonishing feats of valor—Machaon is wounded—Nestor takes him off in his chariot—Achilles sees the two driving toward the camp and sends Patroclus to ask who the wounded man is—This is the beginning of evil for Patroclus—Nestor makes a long speech.

Dawn was rising from her couch beside Tithonus, bringing light to mortals and immortals alike, when Zeus sent fierce Discord to the ships of the Achaeans, with the ensign of war in her hands. She stopped beside the huge black hull of Odysseus’s ship, which lay in the middle of the line, so that her voice would carry farthest in both directions: toward the tents of Ajax son of Telamon on one side, and toward those of Achilles on the other. These two heroes, sure of their own strength, had bravely drawn up their ships at the two ends of the line. There she stood and gave a cry, loud and shrill, that filled the Achaeans with courage. It gave them heart to fight steadily and with all their might, and they would sooner stay and do battle than sail home in their ships.

The son of Atreus shouted aloud and told the Argives to gird themselves for battle, while he put on his own armor. First he fastened his fine greaves around his legs, with ankle-clasps of silver. Then he put on the breastplate that Cinyras had once given him as a guest-gift. News had spread as far as Cyprus that the Achaeans were about to sail for Troy, and that was why Cinyras gave it to the king. It had ten courses of dark cyanus, twelve of gold, and ten of tin. Serpents of cyanus reared up toward the neck, three on each side, like the rainbows that the son of Cronus has set in heaven as a sign to mortal men. Over his shoulders he slung his sword, studded with bosses of gold; its scabbard was silver, with a chain of gold to hang it by. He also took up his richly decorated shield, which covered his body in battle. It was fair to see, with ten circles of bronze running all round it. On the body of the shield were twenty bosses of white tin, with one of dark cyanus in the middle. This center boss was made to show a Gorgon’s head, fierce and grim, with Rout and Panic on either side. The band for the arm to go through was silver, and on it was a writhing snake of cyanus with three heads that sprang from a single neck and wound in and out among one another. On his head Agamemnon set a helmet with a peak in front and behind, and four plumes of horsehair nodded menacingly above it. Then he took two formidable bronze-shod spears. The gleam of his armor shot up from him like a flame into the sky, while Hera and Athena thundered in honor of the king of rich Mycene.

Each man now left his horses with his charioteer, to hold them ready by the trench, and went into battle on foot in full armor. A mighty uproar rose into the dawn. The chiefs were armed and at the trench before the horses got there; the horses came up soon after. The son of Cronus sent an evil portent through their host: the dew fell red with blood, for he was about to send many a brave man hurrying down to Hades.

On the other side, on the rising slope of the plain, the Trojans gathered around great Hector, noble Polydamas, and Aeneas, whom the Trojans honored like an immortal. With them were the three sons of Antenor, Polybus, Agenor, and young Acamas, beautiful as a god. Hector’s round shield showed in the front rank. As a baneful star shines for a moment through a rent in the clouds and is hidden again beneath them, so Hector was seen now in the front ranks and now in the rearmost, and his bronze armor gleamed like the lightning of aegis-bearing Zeus.

As a band of reapers mow swathes of wheat or barley on a rich man’s land, and the sheaves fall thick before them, so the Trojans and Achaeans attacked one another. Neither side would yield; they fought like wolves, and neither got the better of the other. Discord was glad as she watched them, for she was the only god among them. The others were not there; they sat quietly, each in his own home, among the dells and valleys of Olympus. All of them blamed the son of Cronus for wanting to give victory to the Trojans, but father Zeus paid them no heed. He held aloof from them all and sat apart in his all-glorious majesty, looking down on the city of the Trojans, the ships of the Achaeans, the gleam of bronze, and the slayers and the slain alike.

So long as the day was growing and it was still morning, their darts rained thick on both sides and men died. But when the hour came near at which a woodman working in some mountain forest gets his midday meal—for he has felled trees until his hands are weary, he is tired out, and must now have food—then the Danaans, with a cry that rang through all their ranks, broke the enemy battalions. Agamemnon led them on. He killed Bienor first, a leader of his people, and then Bienor’s comrade and charioteer Oileus, who sprang down from his chariot and came straight at him. Agamemnon struck him on the forehead with his spear. His bronze visor was no use against the weapon, which pierced bronze and bone together, so that his brains were battered in and he died in the thick of the fight.

Agamemnon stripped the shirts from their bodies and left them lying where they had fallen, their breasts bare. Then he went on to kill Isus and Antiphus, two sons of Priam, one a bastard and the other born in wedlock. They rode in the same chariot, the bastard driving while noble Antiphus fought beside him. Achilles had once taken both of them prisoner in the glades of Ida, as they were shepherding, and had bound them with fresh withes, but he had accepted a ransom for them. Now Agamemnon son of Atreus struck Isus in the chest, above the nipple, with his spear, and hit Antiphus hard by the ear and threw him from his chariot. At once he stripped off their fine armor, and he recognized them, for he had seen them at the ships when Achilles brought them in from Ida. Just as a lion fastens on the fawns of a hind and crushes them in his great jaws, robbing them of their tender life as he goes back to his lair—and the hind can do nothing for them even if she is close by, for she is in an agony of fear and flees through the thick forest, sweating, at her utmost speed before the mighty beast—so no man of the Trojans could help Isus and Antiphus, for they were themselves fleeing in panic before the Argives.

Then King Agamemnon took the two sons of Antimachus, Pisander and brave Hippolochus. Antimachus had been the foremost in preventing Helen from being given back to Menelaus, since Paris had bribed him heavily. Now Agamemnon caught his two sons in the same chariot, trying to bring their horses to a stand. They had lost hold of the reins, and the horses were mad with fear. The son of Atreus sprang at them like a lion, and the pair begged him from their chariot. “Take us alive, son of Atreus,” they cried, “and you will receive a great ransom for us. Our father Antimachus has a great store of gold, bronze, and wrought iron, and from it he will pay you a very large ransom if he hears that we are alive at the ships of the Achaeans.”

They begged the king with such piteous words and tears, but the answer they heard was not pitying. “If you are sons of Antimachus,” said Agamemnon, “who once proposed at a council of the Trojans that Menelaus and Odysseus, who had come to you as envoys, should be killed and not allowed to return, then you will now pay for your father’s foul wickedness.”

As he spoke he struck Pisander in the chest with his spear and felled him from his chariot to the earth, so that he lay face upward on the ground. Hippolochus fled, but Agamemnon struck him down too. He cut off his hands and his head, and sent the head rolling in among the crowd like a ball. He left them both lying there and flew to wherever the ranks were thickest, while the other Achaeans followed. Foot soldiers drove the enemy foot soldiers in rout before them and killed them, and horsemen did the same to horsemen, while the thundering tramp of the horses raised a cloud of dust from the plain. King Agamemnon came after them, always slaying and cheering on the Achaeans. As when some mighty forest is all ablaze, and the eddying gusts whirl the fire in all directions until the thickets shrivel and are consumed before the blast of the flame, so the heads of the fleeing Trojans fell before Agamemnon son of Atreus. Many a noble pair of horses drew an empty chariot along the highways of war, for want of drivers who lay on the plain, more use now to vultures than to their wives.

Zeus drew Hector away from the darts and dust, the carnage and the din of battle, but the son of Atreus rushed on, calling out loudly to the Danaans. They sped past the tomb of old Ilus, son of Dardanus, in the middle of the plain, and past the wild fig tree, always making for the city, with the son of Atreus still shouting and his hands all smeared with gore. When they reached the Scaean gates and the oak tree, they halted and waited for the others to come up. Meanwhile the Trojans kept fleeing over the middle of the plain like a herd of cows maddened with fright when a lion attacks them in the dead of night. He springs on one of them, seizes her neck in the grip of his strong teeth, laps up her blood, and gorges himself on her entrails. In the same way King Agamemnon son of Atreus pursued the enemy, always slaughtering the hindmost as they fled pell-mell before him. Many a man was flung headlong from his chariot by the hand of the son of Atreus, for he wielded his spear with fury.

But when Agamemnon was just about to reach the high wall and the city, the father of gods and men came down from heaven and sat on the crest of many-fountained Ida, with a thunderbolt in his hand. He told Iris of the golden wings to carry a message for him. “Go, swift Iris,” he said, “and tell Hector this. As long as he sees Agamemnon at the head of his men, making havoc of the Trojan ranks, he is to keep aloof and tell the others to bear the brunt of the battle. But when Agamemnon is wounded by spear or arrow and takes to his chariot, then I will grant Hector strength to slay until he reaches the ships and night falls at the going down of the sun.”

Iris listened and obeyed. She went down from the crests of Ida to strong Ilium, where she found Hector son of Priam standing by his chariot and horses. “Hector son of Priam,” she said, “peer of gods in counsel, father Zeus has sent me with this message for you. While you see Agamemnon leading his men and making havoc of the Trojan ranks, keep aloof and tell the others to bear the brunt of the battle. But once Agamemnon is wounded by spear or arrow and takes to his chariot, Zeus will grant you strength to slay, until you reach the ships and night falls at the going down of the sun.”

Having said this, Iris left him. Hector leaped fully armed from his chariot to the ground. He went all through the host, brandishing his spear, urging his men to fight and stirring up the dread strife of battle. The Trojans wheeled round to face the Achaeans again, and the Argives on their side strengthened their battalions. Now the battle lines were drawn and the two sides stood face to face, with Agamemnon pressing ahead of everyone in his eagerness to be first.

Tell me now, you Muses who dwell in the mansions of Olympus: who, of the Trojans or their allies, was first to face Agamemnon? It was Iphidamas son of Antenor, a man both brave and of great stature, who was brought up in fertile Thrace, the mother of sheep. Cisses, his mother’s father, raised him in his own house when he was a child—Cisses, father of fair Theano. When Iphidamas reached manhood, Cisses wanted to keep him there and was ready to give him his daughter in marriage. But as soon as he was married, he set out to fight the Achaeans with the twelve ships that followed him. He had left these at Percote and come on by land to Ilium. This was the man who now met Agamemnon son of Atreus. When they were close to each other, the son of Atreus missed his aim, and Iphidamas hit him on the girdle below the cuirass, then threw himself on him, trusting in the strength of his arm. But the girdle was not pierced, not nearly, for the point of the spear struck against the silver and was turned aside as though it were lead. King Agamemnon caught the spear and, with the fury of a lion, pulled it toward him out of Iphidamas’s hand. Then he drew his sword and killed Iphidamas by striking him on the neck. So the poor fellow lay there, sleeping a sleep as it were of bronze, killed in defense of his fellow citizens, far from his wedded wife, of whom he had had no joy though he had given much for her. He had paid a hundred head of cattle down and had promised later to give a thousand sheep and goats mixed, from the countless flocks he owned. Agamemnon son of Atreus then despoiled him and carried his armor off into the host of the Achaeans.

When noble Coon, Antenor’s eldest son, saw this, his eyes were sore at the sight of his fallen brother. Unseen by Agamemnon, he got beside him, spear in hand, and wounded him in the middle of the arm below the elbow, so that the point of the spear went right through the arm. Agamemnon shuddered with pain, but even so he did not leave off struggling and fighting. He grasped his spear, which flew swift as the wind, and sprang upon Coon. Coon was trying to drag off the body of his brother, his father’s son, by the foot, and was crying for help to all the bravest of his comrades. Agamemnon struck him with a bronze-shod spear and killed him as he dragged the dead body through the press of men under cover of his shield. Then, standing over the body of Iphidamas, he cut off Coon’s head. So the sons of Antenor met their fate at the hands of the son of Atreus and went down into the house of Hades.

While the blood still ran warm from his wound, Agamemnon kept charging the enemy ranks with spear and sword and great handfuls of stone. Then the bleeding stopped and the wound dried, and the pain grew terrible. A woman in labor is sent sharp pangs by the Eilithuiae, the goddesses of childbirth, who are daughters of Hera and dispense cruel pain. The pangs that struck the son of Atreus were as sharp as those. He leaped onto his chariot and ordered his charioteer to drive to the ships, because he was in great agony. In a loud clear voice he called out to the Danaans, “My friends, princes and counselors of the Argives, you must defend the ships yourselves. Zeus has not allowed me to fight the whole day through against the Trojans.”
